# Explicit Padé and Borel–Padé uniform guarantees

Prepared 2026-09-06. This note supplies sufficient conditions and complete proofs; it does not assert that the neural population kernel satisfies any Stieltjes condition.

Throughout, [p/q] means numerator degree at most p and denominator degree at most q, with denominator normalized to 1 at the origin. Some older papers reverse this convention.

## 1. Compactly supported Stieltjes functions: explicit uniform rate

Let μ be a finite positive measure supported in [0,R], with R>0 and mass m₀. Put

\[
F(t)=\int_{[0,R]}\frac{d\mu(x)}{1+tx},\qquad
m_p=\int x^p\,d\mu(x).
\]

The Taylor coefficients at 0 are c_p=(-1)^p m_p. For infinite support, its [M−1/M] Padé approximant exists for every M≥1 and has the form

\[
R_M(t)=\sum_{j=1}^M\frac{w_j}{1+t x_j},
\quad 0<x_j<R,\quad w_j>0,\quad\sum_jw_j=m_0.
\]

The x_j,w_j are the M-point Gaussian quadrature nodes and weights for μ. Only moments m₀,…,m_(2M−1), equivalently the first 2M Taylor coefficients, are needed. There are no poles on [0,∞). For every T<∞,

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|F(t)-R_M(t)|
\le 2m_0\left(\frac{RT}{2+RT}\right)^{2M}.
\tag{1}
\]

Thus for any ε>0, a finite M suffices on any prescribed compact positive interval, even when T exceeds the radius of the original Taylor expansion. When μ has finitely many support points, its Stieltjes transform is already rational and the hierarchy terminates with exact recovery (allowing deficient degrees).

**Proof of the quadrature and Padé assertions.** Form the monic orthogonal polynomial p_M of degree M. It is determined by its M orthogonality equations against 1,x,…,x^(M−1), whose coefficients involve precisely moments through degree 2M−1. Positive definiteness of the moment matrix follows because a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish on infinite support.

The usual sign-change argument puts M distinct roots x_j in the interior of the convex hull of the support: if there were fewer sign-changing roots there, multiply p_M by the product of their linear factors. The resulting integrand has constant sign and is nonzero on a positive-mass set, while orthogonality says its integral is zero. This contradiction supplies all M distinct roots.

Let ℓ_j be the Lagrange polynomial of degree M−1 at these roots and set w_j=∫ℓ_j dμ. For every polynomial p of degree at most 2M−1, divide p=q p_M+r with deg q,deg r≤M−1. Orthogonality kills the q p_M integral, and interpolation of r gives

\[
\int p\,d\mu=\sum_jw_jp(x_j).
\]

Apply this identity to ℓ_j²: w_j=∫ℓ_j²dμ>0. Apply it to 1 to obtain the mass identity. Expanding each 1/(1+tx_j) formally at zero shows that R_M matches coefficients through degree 2M−1, hence is [M−1/M]. Its rational numerator and denominator have the stated degree bounds. The nodes are positive, so all poles lie on the negative real axis.

**Proof of (1).** For t≥0, put a=1+tR/2 and y=t(x−R/2)/a. Then |y|≤q_t=tR/(2+tR)<1, and the degree-(2M−1) polynomial

\[
p_t(x)=a^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{2M-1}(-y)^j
\]

satisfies

\[
\sup_{x\in[0,R]}\left|\frac1{1+tx}-p_t(x)\right|
\le\frac{q_t^{2M}}{a(1-q_t)}=q_t^{2M}.
\]

Quadrature is exact for p_t. Integrate the error against μ and the quadrature measure, each of mass m₀, to get 2m₀q_t^(2M). Maximizing over t≤T proves (1).

The quadrature–Padé correspondence is classical; an original reference is Allen, Chui, Madych, Narcowich and Smith, [“Padé approximation and gaussian quadrature”](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/133CD9E0E6960B585002005424549ADA/S0004972700043641a.pdf/pade-approximation-and-gaussian-quadrature.pdf), Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society 11 (1974), 63–69. The elementary rate (1) is derived here rather than quoted.

## 2. Zero Taylor radius is also compatible with uniform Padé convergence

Let μ instead be a finite positive measure on [0,∞), with every moment finite, and assume its Stieltjes moment problem is determinate: no other positive measure on [0,∞) has the same moments. Define F and R_M exactly as above using Gaussian quadrature. Then

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|F(t)-R_M(t)|\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{for every finite }T.
\tag{2}
\]

No positive Taylor radius is assumed.

**Proof including the endpoint t=0.** Let μ_M=∑w_jδ_(x_j). Its mass is m₀, and for M≥1 its first moment is m₁. The bound μ_M([A,∞))≤m₁/A gives tightness. Every subsequence has a further weakly convergent subsequence. For each fixed integer p≥1, quadrature eventually matches both moments p and p+1, and

\[
\int_{x>A}x^p\,d\mu_M\le m_{p+1}/A.
\]

This uniform tail estimate allows the p-th moment to pass to the weak limit. Mass passes by tightness. Every such limit therefore has the moments of μ, and determinacy identifies it with μ. Thus μ_M converges weakly to μ.

For every t>0, x↦1/(1+tx) is bounded and continuous, so R_M(t)→F(t). At t=0 they agree exactly. Finally,

\[
|R_M(t)-R_M(s)|\le m_1|t-s|,
\qquad |F(t)-F(s)|\le m_1|t-s|
\]

for nonnegative s,t. A finite mesh of [0,T] and these common Lipschitz bounds upgrade pointwise convergence to uniform convergence. This proves (2).

A convenient sufficient condition for Stieltjes moment determinacy is Carleman's condition

\[
\sum_{p=1}^{\infty}m_p^{-1/(2p)}=\infty.
\tag{3}
\]

In particular, m_p≤C^(p+1)(2p)! suffices. This version and the corresponding Padé convergence statements are recorded in Borghi and Weniger, [“Convergence Analysis of the Summation of the Euler Series by Padé Approximants and the Delta Transformation”](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.2474), §3.1, equations (3.7)–(3.8). The uniform inclusion of t=0 in (2) was proved directly above.

**Example: the Euler series.** Take μ(dx)=e^(−x)dx. Then

\[
F(t)=\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-x}}{1+tx}\,dx,
\qquad F(t)\sim\sum_{p=0}^{\infty}(-1)^pp!t^p.
\]

Differentiation under the integral gives F^(p)(0)=(-1)^p(p!)², as right derivatives. The formal Taylor series diverges for every t>0. Nevertheless, m_p=p! satisfies (3), and the genuine [M−1/M] Padé approximants converge uniformly on every [0,T]. Here F is smooth from the right at 0 but is not analytic there.

Its ordinary Borel transform is especially simple:

\[
\mathcal B F(\xi)=\sum_{p\ge0}(-1)^p\xi^p=\frac1{1+\xi}.
\]

Its [0/1] Padé approximant is already exact, and Borel–Laplace inversion recovers F:

\[
F(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,\mathcal B F(tu)\,du.
\]

Thus this one example has both direct Padé recovery and Borel–Padé recovery despite zero Taylor radius.

## 3. Explicit Borel–Padé uniform recovery when the transform is Stieltjes

Suppose the formal coefficients a_p have a generalized Borel transform

\[
B(\xi)=\sum_{p\ge0}\frac{a_p}{\Gamma(1+\sigma p)}\xi^p
=\int_{[0,R]}\frac{d\mu(x)}{1+\xi x},\qquad \sigma>0,
\]

where μ is positive and finite. Assume the target function is identified with the corresponding Borel sum,

\[
F(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}B(tu^\sigma)\,du.
\tag{4}
\]

This identification is a substantive assumption if F was originally defined by another problem. Conditions on jets alone cannot exclude an added function flat at zero.

Let B_M=[M−1/M]_B and define

\[
F_M(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}B_M(tu^\sigma)\,du.
\]

Only a₀,…,a_(2M−1) enter B_M. Positivity gives 0≤B,B_M≤m₀ on the whole positive ray. For every U>0,

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|F(t)-F_M(t)|
\le 2m_0\left[
\left(\frac{RTU^\sigma}{2+RTU^\sigma}\right)^{2M}
+e^{-U}\right].
\tag{5}
\]

Indeed, split the Laplace integral at U. On [0,U] apply (1) with argument bound TU^σ; on (U,∞) use |B−B_M|≤2m₀. Choose U large enough for the tail, then M large enough for the first term. This proves uniform recovery on every finite [0,T], with an explicit finite-order choice.

For example, for 0<ε<4m₀, choose U=log(4m₀/ε). If RT>0, it suffices to choose

\[
M\ge
\frac{\log(4m_0/\varepsilon)}
{2\log\!\left((2+RTU^\sigma)/(RTU^\sigma)\right)}.
\]

The formula includes exact integration of a rational transform. F_M is a Borel–Padé approximation; it is generally not itself rational in t and need not be a Padé approximant to the original series. If a finite rational expression in t is desired, cut the integral at U and use finite positive quadrature there. Uniform continuity of (t,u)↦e^(−u)B_M(tu^σ) on [0,T]×[0,U] gives uniform quadrature convergence. The resulting finite sum is rational in t, with no nonnegative poles, but is not in general a classical Padé approximant to the original series.

There is also a direct Padé consequence under a moderate exponent. By Tonelli, (4) is itself the Stieltjes transform of the measure obtained by sending (x,u) to xu^σ under μ(dx)e^(−u)du. Its moments are

\[
\Gamma(1+\sigma p)m_p\le m_0R^p\Gamma(1+\sigma p).
\]

If 0<σ≤2, condition (3) follows from Stirling's formula, because the Carleman terms are bounded below by a constant times p^(−σ/2). Thus direct [M−1/M] Padé approximants to the original formal series also converge uniformly on every [0,T]. For σ>2, this sufficient argument stops; (5) still proves Borel–Padé convergence under the stated transform and identification assumptions.

## 4. An explicit coefficient condition for the compact-support hypothesis

Write b_p=a_p/Γ(1+σp). For a declared R>0 put s_p=(-1)^p b_p/R^p. The condition

\[
\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^j\binom{k}{j}s_{p+j}\ge0
\quad\text{for all integers }p,k\ge0
\tag{6}
\]

is equivalent to existence of a finite positive measure ν on [0,1] with s_p=∫x^p dν(x). This is the Hausdorff moment criterion. Scaling ν by x↦Rx gives exactly the compactly supported Stieltjes representation for B above. The mass is s₀=b₀. The zero-mass case gives the identically zero transform.

For a primary modern mathematical source, see Liu and Pego, [“On generating functions of Hausdorff moment sequences”](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.8052), or Diaconis and Freedman, [“The Markov moment problem and de Finetti's theorem: Part I”](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/users/freedman/631.pdf), Theorem 1. In (6), positivity follows in the forward direction by integrating x^p(1−x)^k. The reverse direction is Hausdorff's theorem.

This is an all-orders condition, not a finite collection of successful sign tests. It proves a structural sufficient condition for the transform, but it still does not by itself identify a separately specified population-GF observable with its Borel sum.

# Uniform Borel–Padé transfer and an explicit finite-jet rational alternative

Prepared 6 September 2026. This note proves conditional reconstruction statements. It does not establish the Borel reconstruction premise for the population gradient flow.

## 1. Exact hypotheses for transferring Borel-plane approximation

Fix \(\sigma>0\) and \(T>0\). Suppose the actual function of interest satisfies

\[
f(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}B(tu^\sigma)\,du,
\qquad 0\le t\le T.
\]

Here \(B\) is continuous on the nonnegative ray and is analytic near zero with coefficients

\[
B(\xi)=\sum_{p\ge0}b_p\xi^p,
\qquad b_p=\frac{c_p}{\Gamma(1+\sigma p)}.
\]

The \(c_p\) may be formal Taylor coefficients obtained from initialization derivatives. The displayed integral identity is an assumption about the actual target function, not a consequence merely of the existence of these coefficients.

Let \(R_N\) be rational approximants constructed from finitely many \(b_p\). They can be ordinary Padé approximants when a separate Padé convergence theorem applies. Suppose

\[
\varepsilon_N(L):=\sup_{0\le\xi\le L}|R_N(\xi)-B(\xi)|\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{for each finite }L.
\]

In particular, the approximants eventually have no nonremovable poles on each specified compact segment.

Assume also a common growth bound

\[
|R_N(\xi)|+|B(\xi)|\le C\exp(b\xi^{1/\sigma}),
\quad \xi\ge0,
\quad b\ge0,
\]

and put \(\lambda=1-bT^{1/\sigma}>0\). The reconstructed functions

\[
f_N(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}R_N(tu^\sigma)\,du
\]

then converge uniformly to \(f\) on \([0,T]\).

Indeed, for every \(U>0\), splitting the integral at \(U\) gives the explicit estimate

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|f_N(t)-f(t)|
\le
(1-e^{-U})\varepsilon_N(TU^\sigma)
+\frac C\lambda e^{-\lambda U}.
\]

On the finite part, \(tu^\sigma\in[0,TU^\sigma]\). On the tail,

\[
e^{-u}\bigl(|R_N(tu^\sigma)|+|B(tu^\sigma)|\bigr)
\le Ce^{-(1-bt^{1/\sigma})u}
\le Ce^{-\lambda u}.
\]

Choose \(U\) first to make the tail small, and then \(N\) to make the finite part small. This proves uniform convergence, including \(t=0\).

This proof uses no independent values of the target at positive times. However, a guaranteed computable choice of \(N\) requires a known bound on \(\varepsilon_N(L)\); qualitative convergence alone provides an existence statement.

## 2. A weaker and more practical theorem using a cutoff

The common global growth bound on all \(R_N\) is unnecessary if the approximation uses a finite Laplace cutoff. Assume only

\[
|B(\xi)|\le C e^{b\xi^{1/\sigma}},
\qquad \lambda=1-bT^{1/\sigma}>0,
\]

and the local uniform convergence of \(R_N\) stated above. Define

\[
f_{N,U}(t)=\int_0^U e^{-u}R_N(tu^\sigma)\,du.
\]

Then

\[
\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|f_{N,U}(t)-f(t)|
\le (1-e^{-U})\varepsilon_N(TU^\sigma)
+\frac C\lambda e^{-\lambda U}.
\]

The proof estimates the true \(B\) tail only. Thus even poles of \(R_N\) farther along the positive ray are irrelevant, provided none lie on the compact segment used by the cutoff.

For every \(\epsilon>0\), choose \(U\) so that the last term is at most \(\epsilon/3\), then choose a finite \(N\) so that the first term is at most \(\epsilon/3\). One can choose an increasing-cutoff diagonal sequence with error tending to zero, but no arbitrary rule \(U=U_N\to\infty\) is justified by compact convergence alone: approximation quality must also be controlled on the growing segment \([0,TU_N^\sigma]\).

More generally, the exponential growth hypothesis can be replaced by any uniform true-tail estimate

\[
\sup_{t\le T}\int_U^\infty e^{-u}|B(tu^\sigma)|\,du\longrightarrow0.
\]

## 3. Finite quadrature really gives a finite construction

Fix \(U,N\) as above. Partition \([0,U]\) into subintervals with mesh at most \(h\), choose a sample point \(v_j\) in each, and let

\[
w_j=\int_{u_{j-1}}^{u_j}e^{-u}\,du.
\]

The finite approximation is

\[
\widetilde f_{N,U,Q}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^Qw_j R_N(tv_j^\sigma).
\]

Because \((t,u)\mapsto R_N(tu^\sigma)\) is continuous on the compact rectangle \([0,T]\times[0,U]\), these weighted Riemann sums converge uniformly in \(t\) as the mesh shrinks.

There is also an elementary explicit bound. If

\[
D_N=\sup_{0\le\xi\le TU^\sigma}|R_N'(\xi)|<\infty,
\]

then the quadrature error is at most

\[
D_NT
\begin{cases}
h^\sigma,&0<\sigma\le1,\\
\sigma U^{\sigma-1}h,&\sigma\ge1.
\end{cases}
\]

The bound follows by the mean-value estimate for \(R_N\), the Hölder estimate for \(u^\sigma\) when \(\sigma\le1\), and the derivative bound for \(u^\sigma\) when \(\sigma\ge1\). The weights have total mass \(1-e^{-U}\le1\).

Choose finite \(Q\) to make this error at most \(\epsilon/3\). Then the preceding choices of \(U,N,Q\) give

\[
\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|\widetilde f_{N,U,Q}(t)-f(t)|\le\epsilon.
\]

If \(R_N\) is rational in its argument, the finite sum is rational in \(t\). Its coefficients depend on finitely many initialization coefficients, the declared reconstruction constants, and the quadrature rule. Its degree generally grows with both \(N\) and \(Q\).

This rational function is generally **not** the direct conventional \([m/n]\) Padé approximant of \(f\): its construction approximates the Borel transform and then approximates the Laplace integral. In particular, finite cutoff/quadrature need not preserve the exact initialization Taylor matching conditions. Uniform function approximation is the conclusion.

## 4. An explicit alternative that guarantees rational reconstruction

The preceding theorems intentionally separate Borel summability from rational approximation of \(B\). Merely knowing that \(B\) is analytic along the positive ray does not by itself establish uniform convergence of a chosen ordinary diagonal Padé sequence.

A known analytic domain gives a constructive alternative. Suppose \(B\) is analytic in

\[
D_a=\{\xi\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}\xi>-a\},\qquad a>0.
\]

The explicit maps

\[
w=\frac{\xi}{\xi+2a},
\qquad
\xi=\frac{2aw}{1-w}
\]

map \(D_a\) biholomorphically to the unit disk and back. Therefore

\[
G(w)=B\left(\frac{2aw}{1-w}\right)
=\sum_{j\ge0}g_jw^j
\]

is analytic for \(|w|<1\). Its first \(N+1\) coefficients require only the first \(N+1\) coefficients of \(B\):

\[
g_0=b_0,
\qquad
g_j=\sum_{k=1}^j b_k(2a)^k\binom{j-1}{k-1}
\quad(j\ge1).
\]

Define

\[
R_N(\xi)=\sum_{j=0}^N g_j\left(\frac{\xi}{\xi+2a}\right)^j.
\]

This is a rational function whose only possible pole is \(-2a\), and it is computable from a finite jet at zero. For any \(L<\infty\), put \(q=L/(L+2a)<1\), choose \(q<r<1\), and let

\[
M_r=\max_{|w|=r}\left|B\left(\frac{2aw}{1-w}\right)\right|.
\]

Cauchy's coefficient bound \(|g_j|\le M_r r^{-j}\) gives

\[
\sup_{0\le\xi\le L}|B(\xi)-R_N(\xi)|
\le
\frac{M_r(q/r)^{N+1}}{1-q/r}.
\]

Thus local uniform rational approximation is guaranteed with an explicit geometric error. If a numerical bound on \(M_r\) is given, this is an effective finite-order estimate. For example, the stronger hypothesis

\[
|B(\xi)|\le C e^{b|\xi|}\quad(\xi\in D_a)
\]

implies \(M_r\le C\exp(2ab r/(1-r))\), yielding a completely explicit bound. In the ordinary \(\sigma=1\) Borel case, the same hypothesis supplies the true-ray tail estimate for every \(T<1/b\), with no time restriction from this bound if \(b=0\).

Combining this rational construction with Sections 2–3 proves the requested finite-initialization-data, uniform-on-\([0,T]\) approximation property under explicit analytic-domain, growth, and Borel-identification hypotheses.

The approximation is Taylor truncation in a conformal coordinate, hence a rational or Padé-type construction in \(\xi\). It is **not** generally ordinary \([N/N]\) Padé approximation: it matches the available \(N+1\) Taylor coefficients, rather than imposing the usual \(2N+1\) matching conditions. This distinction must remain explicit.

The general reconstruction framework appears in Costin–Dunne, *Uniformization and Constructive Analytic Continuation of Taylor Series*, Theorem 8, pp. 6–7: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.01962. It gives finite-coefficient reconstruction using a known uniformizing map and bounds dictated by the analytic domain. The elementary half-plane specialization above is proved directly, so no further hypotheses from their Riemann-surface theorem are being silently imported.

## 5. Implication for the GF conjecture and limits of the claim

For the population GF program, first establish that the actual scalar observable, output-dependent kernel, or matrix kernel equals the asserted Borel–Laplace sum. Establishing existence of the population GF and computing its initialization derivatives does not establish that identity.

Then either a genuine Padé convergence theorem for the relevant Borel transform or an explicit conformal reconstruction theorem can supply finite initialization-based approximations uniformly on a fixed positive interval. Existing prediction stability estimates and the established joint width/GD theorem can transfer this to network predictions and losses.

No all-time conclusion follows without global continuation and tail control. No general positive-ray Padé convergence theorem has been proved here from Gevrey coefficient bounds alone. No effective complexity guarantee follows from qualitative convergence unless its constants and convergence modulus can be controlled.

# One-point Padé: verified analytic guarantees and their limits

Research note, 6 September 2026. This note supplies exact sufficient conditions and prevents overreading general Padé convergence results. It does not assert that a neural population observable has the required analytic continuation or Borel-summability properties.

## Definition and distinct approximation questions

For a formal series \(F(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jz^j\), a Padé pair of type \([p/q]\) satisfies

\[
\deg P\le p,\quad \deg Q\le q,\quad Q\not\equiv0,
\qquad QF-P=O(z^{p+q+1}).
\]

The rational function \(P/Q\) is unique although the polynomial pair need not be unique. When \(Q(0)\ne0\), one normalizes \(Q(0)=1\), and the rational function itself matches the series through degree \(p+q\). Degenerate entries can have common zeros at zero; after cancellation their actual contact order needs care. Under the convergence theorems below the relevant entries are eventually well behaved.

The coefficients used are only \(a_0,\ldots,a_{p+q}\). They can be genuine Taylor coefficients or formal asymptotic coefficients; existence of the algebraic rational approximant does not imply convergence to a given function.

Source for definition/existence/uniqueness and defects: Beckermann and Matos, *Algebraic properties of robust Padé approximants*, arXiv:1310.2438, pp. 1–3, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.2438.

Arbitrary rational approximation is different. Every continuous function on [0,T] is uniformly approximable by polynomials (Bernstein's elementary approximation theorem suffices), hence by rational functions. These approximants use function values or global information and need not be Padé approximants of its initialization jet. A flat nonzero function \(e^{-1/t^2}\), extended by zero at zero, has zero jet, whose normal rational Padé approximants are zero. Thus mere continuous/smooth rational approximability supplies no initialization-jet reconstruction theorem.

## Positive ordinary-Padé theorem: de Montessus fixed row

Suppose F is analytic near zero and has a meromorphic continuation to the disk \(|z|<R\), with exactly q poles there, counted with multiplicity. Fix this denominator degree q and let numerator degree p tend to infinity. Then

\[
[p/q]_F\longrightarrow F
\]

uniformly on each compact subset of that disk avoiding the poles. In particular, if T<R and no pole lies on [0,T], then for every epsilon>0 some finite p gives

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|[p/q]_F(t)-F(t)|<\varepsilon.
\]

The denominators converge to the polynomial with exactly those poles as zeros; hence they have no spurious poles near the compact interval for all sufficiently large p. This theorem does not require that the Taylor disk itself contain [0,T]. Nearby complex poles can limit the Taylor radius and be captured by the fixed-degree denominator.

More exact rate statement: let R_q be the largest meromorphy-disk radius with at most q poles and suppose the disk has exactly q poles. For any compact K avoiding them,

\[
\limsup_{p\to\infty}\|F-[p/q]_F\|_K^{1/p}
\le \frac{\max_{z\in K}|z|}{R_q}<1.
\]

The inequality is sufficient here; the cited paper gives a sharp formulation. Its notation \(\pi_{n,q}\) means numerator degree n−q, so substitute n=p+q when comparing statements.

Verified source: Cacoq, de la Calle Ysern and López Lagomasino, *Incomplete Padé approximation and convergence of row sequences of Hermite-Padé approximants*, arXiv:1111.2774, p. 2, named “Montessus de Ballore Theorem,” https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.2774. The paper defines R_q on p. 1 and explicitly states compact sup-norm convergence and pole attraction. Published J. Approx. Theory 170 (2013), 59–77, DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jat.2012.05.005.

Simple example, independently checked:

\[
F(t)=\frac1{1+t},\qquad
\sum_{j\ge0}(-t)^j\text{ diverges for }t>1,
\qquad [0/1]_F(t)=F(t).
\]

Thus failure of Taylor partial sums on [0,T] can coexist with exact finite Padé reconstruction. This example is analytic at zero and does not address a zero-radius asymptotic series.

## Stahl's theorem is weaker than the requested supremum norm

A safe relevant specialization: for an analytic germ with continuation along paths avoiding a finite set of branch points (more generally the appropriate compact set of zero logarithmic capacity), diagonal/near-diagonal Padé approximants converge in logarithmic capacity in a distinguished domain of single-valued continuation, determined through a minimum-capacity cut. This is not uniform convergence on every compact subset. Tiny exceptional sets may contain poles; even one genuine approximant pole in [0,T] makes the supremum error unbounded.

Primary source: Herbert Stahl, *The Convergence of Padé Approximants to Functions with Branch Points*, J. Approx. Theory 91 (1997), 139–204, DOI https://doi.org/10.1006/jath.1997.3141, publisher https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021904597931415. Its abstract explicitly says convergence in capacity, describes the zero-capacity singularity-set condition and near-diagonal degrees, and identifies the extremal domain. One should not quote a generic internet description saying “Padé converges to the maximal analytic continuation” as a compact-uniform theorem.

An additional usable condition: if such capacity convergence is known in a domain D and all sufficiently late rational approximants have no poles in an open subdomain U, then Gonchar's lemma gives locally uniform convergence in U (for the holomorphic limit). In particular take an open neighborhood U of [0,R]. Pole avoidance only on the real interval is not the same as absence of poles in a complex neighborhood.

Verified source: Beckermann–Matos, arXiv:1310.2438, abstract and p. 2, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.2438. They state capacity plus absence of poles implies locally uniform convergence and cite Gonchar's 1975 lemma. They also exhibit an SVD-robust Padé approximant with spurious poles, so numerical robustness alone is not this hypothesis. Cacoq et al. pp. 4–5 give the related theorem with one-dimensional Hausdorff content, explicitly distinguishing it from the logarithmic-capacity terminology.

## Why general analyticity does not guarantee diagonal uniform convergence

The Baker–Gammel–Wills conjecture asserted that every function meromorphic in the unit disk and analytic at zero admits one subsequence of diagonal Padé approximants converging uniformly on all compact subsets of that disk away from the function's poles. Lubinsky disproved this with a Rogers–Ramanujan continued fraction.

Primary source: Doron Lubinsky, *Rogers-Ramanujan and the Baker-Gammel-Wills (Padé) conjecture*, Annals of Mathematics 157 (2003), 847–889, https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2003/157-3/p04, also https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0402305.

Buslaev provided a counterexample even to the holomorphic version and to the corresponding algebraic-function conjecture.

Primary source: V. I. Buslaev, *On the Baker–Gammel–Wills conjecture in the theory of Padé approximants*, Sbornik: Mathematics 193:6 (2002), 811–823, https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/sm658, DOI https://doi.org/10.1070/SM2002v193n06ABEH000658. The publisher abstract explicitly states both failures.

Quantifier caution: these counterexamples refute a universal diagonal subsequence working on all compact subsets of a two-dimensional disk. Do not silently turn that into the stronger claim that every function has a particular real [0,T] on which no selectable finite Padé entry can attain arbitrary accuracy. They suffice to refute the frequently invoked blanket compact-uniform diagonal theorem.

A separate striking full-sequence failure: Wallin constructed an entire function for which limsup_n |[n/n](z)|=infinity for every z≠0; its example also has a good locally uniformly convergent subsequence. Verified authoritative author survey: Lubinsky, *Spurious poles in Padé approximation*, Theorem 3.2, p. 10, https://lubinsky.math.gatech.edu/Research%20papers/SpuriousSavannahSurveyFeb262018.pdf. Original: H. Wallin, *The convergence of Padé approximants and the size of the power series coefficients*, Applicable Analysis 4 (1974), 235–251. Since the original was not read, prefer the Lubinsky/Buslaev primary citations above for the final answer and omit Wallin unless helpful.

## A transparent normal-family sufficient condition

There is an elementary condition independent of special Stieltjes structure. Let B be analytic on a connected complex open set U containing zero and [0,R]. Suppose the rational B_N are holomorphic on U, match the Taylor coefficients of B to orders tending to infinity, and are locally uniformly bounded:

\[
\text{for every compact }K\subset U,\qquad
\sup_N\sup_{z\in K}|B_N(z)|<\infty.
\]

Then B_N→B locally uniformly on U.

Proof: Montel's theorem makes every subsequence have a locally uniformly convergent subsubsequence. Cauchy's formula transfers derivatives at zero to its limit. Growing coefficient contact forces every derivative of that limit to equal B's derivatives. The identity theorem gives equality on connected U. Since every convergent subsubsequence has the same limit, the full sequence converges locally uniformly.

This condition can be obtained from verified numerator/denominator bounds, but boundedness is a substantive hypothesis, not a consequence of Padé matching. This argument applies just as well to a Borel transform B and explains exactly what pole and growth control must achieve.

## Application to Borel–Padé reconstruction

For \(F(t)\sim\sum a_jt^j\) and \(B(\xi)=\sum a_j\xi^j/\Gamma(1+\sigma j)\), Borel summation first needs an actual analytic continuation B and identification

\[
F(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}B(tu^\sigma)\,du.
\]

Padé applied to B is an analytic-continuation procedure. Any above compact-uniform theorem can be applied to B, but the Laplace integral samples an unbounded ray. One also needs tail control, or must truncate the integral at a cutoff chosen using a tail bound for the actual B. Borel summability alone does not invoke de Montessus (no finite-pole meromorphy disk has been supplied), does not forbid Padé spurious poles, and does not turn Stahl capacity convergence into a sup estimate.

For a cutoff U, compact-uniform convergence on \([0,TU^\sigma]\) gives

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left|
\int_0^U e^{-u}[B_N(tu^\sigma)-B(tu^\sigma)]\,du
\right|
\le(1-e^{-U})
\sup_{0\le\xi\le TU^\sigma}|B_N(\xi)-B(\xi)|.
\]

Add a uniformly small tail \(\sup_{t\le T}\int_U^\infty e^{-u}|B(tu^\sigma)|du\). This gives an initialization-jet finite Borel–Padé approximation without needing a global growth bound for B_N. The resulting finite-cutoff integral is generally not a rational function of t; finite quadrature makes it a finite sum of scaled rational functions, which is rational in t and computable from finitely many jets. All orders/cutoffs/quadrature counts are selected for the prescribed epsilon and fixed T.

This is the appropriate logical connection for the PDE project: a verified Padé theorem for the actual Borel transform plus a Borel identity and tail bound closes the remaining approximation implication; none is provided merely by population GF existence.

items.text: The conditions now give an explicit error bound: a finite Padé order can be chosen for any prescribed \(\varepsilon\) and fixed \(T\). The Borel argument also has a useful refinement: truncate the Laplace integral at a controlled cutoff, then approximate the Borel transform only on the finite segment needed by that cutoff. I’ve also verified a separate rational construction based on complex analyticity, for cases where Stieltjes positivity is unavailable.

items.text:
**Yes. There are precise conditions guaranteeing exactly this: for every fixed \(T>0\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), a finite Padé order gives uniform error below \(\varepsilon\), even when the original Taylor series diverges for every \(t>0\).** There are also guarantees for Padé applied to the Borel transform.

The important distinction is between:

- **Direct Padé:** a rational approximation to the original function, computed from its initialization coefficients.
- **Borel–Padé:** a rational approximation to its Borel transform, followed by a reconstruction integral.

These procedures can both converge, but their guarantees require different assumptions.

Write
\[
F(t)\sim\sum_{p\ge0}a_p t^p,
\qquad a_p=\frac{F^{(p)}(0)}{p!}
\]
when these derivatives exist. A Padé approximant \([L/M]_F=P_L/Q_M\) satisfies
\[
Q_M(t)\sum_{p\ge0}a_pt^p-P_L(t)
=O(t^{L+M+1}),
\qquad Q_M(0)=1,
\]
with numerator and denominator degrees at most \(L,M\). Thus it uses finitely many coefficients at initialization.

By “not Taylor approximable,” I mean that these Taylor partial sums fail to approximate \(F\). Arbitrary polynomial approximation is a different question: every continuous function on \([0,T]\) admits that, but the approximating polynomials need not be obtainable from its initialization derivatives.

**A concrete genuine Padé guarantee is available for positive Stieltjes integrals.** Suppose the actual function has the representation
\[
F(t)=\int_{[0,R]}\frac{d\mu(x)}{1+tx},
\qquad \mu\ge0,\qquad m_0=\mu([0,R])<\infty.
\]

Then its \([M-1/M]\) Padé approximant has the form
\[
R_M(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{w_j}{1+tx_j},
\qquad w_j>0,\quad x_j\in[0,R].
\]

The nodes and weights are determined by the first \(2M\) initialization coefficients. All poles are negative, and
\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|F(t)-R_M(t)|
\le
2m_0\left(\frac{RT}{2+RT}\right)^{2M}.
\tag{1}
\]

Because \(RT/(2+RT)<1\) for every finite \(T\), this gives your requested guarantee. For \(0<\varepsilon<2m_0\), it suffices to choose
\[
M\ge
\frac{\log(2m_0/\varepsilon)}
{2\log\!\bigl((2+RT)/(RT)\bigr)}.
\]

The mechanism is concrete. The Padé approximant is Gaussian quadrature for the displayed integral, exact on polynomials in \(x\) through degree \(2M-1\). Expand
\[
\frac1{1+tx}
=
\frac1{1+tR/2}
\frac1{1+\dfrac{t(x-R/2)}{1+tR/2}}.
\]
The inner ratio has absolute value at most \(RT/(2+RT)\). Truncating its geometric expansion gives a uniformly small polynomial error; integration and quadrature agree on the polynomial. Their two remaining errors give (1). The Padé–quadrature correspondence is classical. [Allen–Chui–Madych–Narcowich–Smith](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0004972700043641)

For example,
\[
F(t)=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+tx}
=\frac{\log(1+t)}{t},\qquad F(0)=1.
\]
Its Taylor series fails for \(t>1\), while (1) guarantees uniform Padé approximation on every finite \([0,T]\).

**Even zero Taylor radius is compatible with uniform Padé convergence.** Consider
\[
F(t)=\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-x}}{1+tx}\,dx.
\]
Its initialization expansion is
\[
F(t)\sim\sum_{p=0}^{\infty}(-1)^p p!\,t^p,
\]
which diverges for every \(t>0\). Nevertheless,
\[
[M-1/M]_F\longrightarrow F
\quad\text{uniformly on every }[0,T].
\]

Here the positive measure has unbounded support, but its moments \(m_p=p!\) determine it uniquely. More generally, positive Stieltjes measures with all moments finite and a **determinate moment problem** have this Padé convergence property. Uniformity includes \(t=0\): both the integral and its quadrature approximants have the common Lipschitz bound \(m_1|t-s|\), which upgrades pointwise convergence to uniform convergence on the compact interval. [Simon, Theorem 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/9906008)

This example also makes the Borel connection especially transparent:
\[
B(\xi)=\sum_{p\ge0}\frac{(-1)^pp!}{p!}\xi^p
=\frac1{1+\xi},
\qquad
F(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}B(tu)\,du.
\]
The \([0/1]\) Padé approximant of \(B\) is already exact. Thus both direct Padé and Borel–Padé recover a function with a divergent Taylor series. [Borghi–Weniger](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.2474)

**The general link is a uniform approximation theorem for the Borel reconstruction integral.** For some \(\sigma>0\), suppose
\[
B(\xi)=
\sum_{p\ge0}\frac{a_p}{\Gamma(1+\sigma p)}\xi^p
\]
converges near zero, continues along the positive ray, and the **actual target** satisfies
\[
F(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}B(tu^\sigma)\,du.
\tag{2}
\]

Suppose Padé approximants \(B_M\), computed from finitely many transformed coefficients, converge uniformly to \(B\) on every finite positive-ray segment. Also suppose the true integral has a uniformly small tail:
\[
E(U):=
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
\int_U^\infty e^{-u}|B(tu^\sigma)|\,du
\longrightarrow0.
\]

Then the finite-cutoff reconstruction satisfies the elementary bound
\[
\sup_{t\le T}
\left|
F(t)-\int_0^U e^{-u}B_M(tu^\sigma)\,du
\right|
\le
E(U)
+
\sup_{0\le\xi\le TU^\sigma}|B(\xi)-B_M(\xi)|.
\tag{3}
\]

This proves the desired quantifiers:

1. Choose a finite \(U\) to make the tail small.
2. Choose a finite \(M\) to approximate \(B\) on \([0,TU^\sigma]\).
3. Approximate the remaining integral by finite quadrature.

The resulting expression
\[
\widetilde F(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_jB_M(tu_j^\sigma)
\]
is a finite rational function of \(t\), with coefficients obtained from initialization data and the declared quadrature rule. It generally is **not** the conventional Padé approximant of the original series: Padé matching was imposed on \(B\).

For an explicit tail condition, it suffices that
\[
|B(\xi)|\le C e^{b\xi^{1/\sigma}},
\qquad b\ge0,\qquad bT^{1/\sigma}<1.
\]
Then \(E(U)\le C e^{-\lambda U}/\lambda\), where \(\lambda=1-bT^{1/\sigma}>0\).

**There are explicit coefficient conditions that make this Borel–Padé argument work.** One sufficient condition is that
\[
B(\xi)=\int_{[0,R]}\frac{d\nu(x)}{1+\xi x},
\qquad \nu\ge0.
\tag{4}
\]

Now the earlier Padé theorem applies to \(B\), and both \(B\) and its approximants are bounded by \(\nu_0=\nu([0,R])\) on the entire positive ray. Assuming (2), their full Laplace reconstructions \(F_M\) satisfy
\[
\sup_{t\le T}|F(t)-F_M(t)|
\le
2\nu_0
\left[
\left(\frac{RTU^\sigma}{2+RTU^\sigma}\right)^{2M}
+e^{-U}
\right].
\tag{5}
\]
Again, choose \(U\), then \(M\). This works for every finite \(T\).

Condition (4) can be expressed directly in the coefficients. Define
\[
s_p=\frac{(-1)^p a_p}
{\Gamma(1+\sigma p)R^p}.
\]
A sufficient—and equivalent compact-moment—condition is
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^j\binom{k}{j}s_{p+j}\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }p,k\ge0.
\tag{6}
\]
These inequalities say that \(s_p\) are moments of a finite positive measure on \([0,1]\); rescaling gives (4). They are **all-order conditions**, so finitely many successful coefficient tests do not establish the theorem. [Liu–Pego on Hausdorff moment sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.8052)

There is an additional direct connection: under (2)–(4), when \(0<\sigma\le2\), genuine \([M-1/M]\) Padé approximants of \(F\) itself also converge uniformly. Indeed, the double integral represents \(F\) as a Stieltjes integral with moments bounded by
\[
\nu_0R^p\Gamma(1+\sigma p).
\]
The Stieltjes Carleman criterion applies because its terms are bounded below by a constant times \(p^{-\sigma/2}\), whose sum diverges for \(\sigma\le2\). Thus the measure is determinate. For larger \(\sigma\), this particular argument stops; the Borel–Padé guarantee (5) still holds.

**Positivity is sufficient, but it is not necessary.** Two other useful routes are:

- **Meromorphic continuation:** if \(F\) is analytic near zero and extends to \(|t|<r\) with exactly \(q\) poles, then the fixed-denominator Padé sequence \([L/q]\), \(L\to\infty\), converges uniformly on compact subsets avoiding those poles. Hence it covers \([0,T]\), \(T<r\), even beyond the Taylor radius. This is the de Montessus theorem. [Precise statement](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.2774)
- **A known analytic domain for \(B\):** a conformal change of variable can give a guaranteed finite-jet rational construction. For example, if \(B\) is analytic in \(\operatorname{Re}\xi>-a\), put
  \[
  w=\frac{\xi}{\xi+2a},
  \qquad
  B\!\left(\frac{2aw}{1-w}\right)=\sum_{p\ge0}g_pw^p.
  \]
  Then \(\sum_{p=0}^{M}g_p[\xi/(\xi+2a)]^p\) converges uniformly on every finite positive-ray segment. Each \(g_p\) uses only the first \(p+1\) Borel coefficients. Combining this with (3) gives the desired finite rational approximation without Stieltjes positivity. This is a conformal rational construction, rather than conventional diagonal Padé. [Costin–Dunne, Theorem 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.01962)

For our population GF problem, these results provide **specific sufficient assumptions that could close the reconstruction conjecture**. We would need to establish the relevant conditions for the actual kernel or prediction observable. Existence of the GF, smoothness, or a factorial coefficient bound alone does not establish them. In particular, equality with the Borel sum in (2) remains essential: initialization derivatives cannot detect an added nonzero flat function.

I wrote the complete statements, proofs, coefficient criteria and their implications for our setting in [Uniform Padé and Borel approximation from initialization jets](/tmp/pde-gf-supervisor-worktree/PADE_BOREL_UNIFORM_APPROXIMATION.md).

# Finite causal neural PDE research

This repository studies whether dense nonlinear feature-learning dynamics can
be represented by a finite, autonomous, causal PDE state.

The dated project-wide baseline is
[`FINITE_CAUSAL_NEURAL_PDE_MASTER_MONOGRAPH_v2.2_2026-07-31.md`](FINITE_CAUSAL_NEURAL_PDE_MASTER_MONOGRAPH_v2.2_2026-07-31.md).
It records the state on 31 July 2026 and does not contain later MFP or
Stieltjes work. The later cross-study orientation is
[`UNIFIED_FINITE_CAUSAL_NEURAL_PDE_SYNTHESIS_2026-08-19.md`](UNIFIED_FINITE_CAUSAL_NEURAL_PDE_SYNTHESIS_2026-08-19.md).
Within each active program, that program's maintained
`CURRENT_RESEARCH_STATE.md` or README-designated current report takes
precedence over the older monograph and historical reports.

## Research map

The repository is organized by scientific question, not by software artifact
type:

| Program | Question |
|---|---|
| [`studies/quadratic_nonclosure`](studies/quadratic_nonclosure/) | What fails in the prescribed quadratic Taylor/Wick closure? |
| [`studies/mean_field_peeling`](studies/mean_field_peeling/) | How can fixed-order μP derivative observables be peeled layer by layer into explicit Gaussian calculations, and which parts are proved or compiled exactly? |
| [`studies/stieltjes_conjecture`](studies/stieltjes_conjecture/) | Does the quadratic-network output kernel define a Stieltjes moment sequence and a convergent rational ODE hierarchy? |
| [`studies/resnet_pde`](studies/resnet_pde/) | How much of the fully connected residual-network dynamics is captured by finite response structure and an explicit finite-source PDE, and what still blocks convergence and dense-limit identification? |

Each program keeps its reports, code, protocols, and evidence together.
Sequential investigations are arranged as phases only when chronology is
scientifically important. Release-only wrappers and exact historical layouts
live in the archive rather than in the active research tree.

## Other material

- [`archive/bundles`](archive/bundles/) contains the original immutable ZIP
  releases.
- [`archive/earlier_documents`](archive/earlier_documents/) contains superseded
  project-wide syntheses and reports.
- [`requirements-lock.txt`](requirements-lock.txt) records the common Python
  environment used for the 31 July numerical execution audit.

There is deliberately no repository-wide `src`, `tests`, `tools`, `releases`,
or `runs` layer. Tests remain beside the experiment they validate, and new
reproductions remain beside the study they reproduce.

# An autonomous law for nonlinear feature learning

## The proved arctangent theorem, the extension program, and the geometry it may reveal

**Repository-level note — 21 August 2026**

This note records a point at which the research program changed character.
The project no longer has only formal derivatives, candidate closures, or
evidence that a compact causal theory might exist. It has one complete
nonlinear theorem.

For a fully trained, two-hidden-layer network with arctangent activation, one
input, squared loss, canonical Gaussian initialization, and the mean-field
feature-learning scaling, the infinite-width training dynamics are governed
by a deterministic, autonomous, restartable integro-differential equation.
Its state has a constant number of field/operator species, every evolving
object has one training-time coordinate, and it contains no response kernel,
second training time, or stored trajectory. On every fixed physical-time
interval, the finite-width predictor, raw tangent kernel, residual, and loss
converge to direct readouts of that current state.

That is the proved result. The extensions to more samples, greater depth,
broader activation classes, and richer observables are research programs,
not consequences already contained in the theorem. The proposed geometric
interpretation of representation learning is separated still more sharply:
part of it is an exact variational consequence of the theorem, while the
Gram-space and optimal-transport interpretation is a conjectural organizing
principle.

The authoritative proof and its audits are:

- [`ARCTAN_THEOREM_AND_PROOF.md`](studies/mean_field_peeling/nonlinear_activation_operator_ide/ARCTAN_THEOREM_AND_PROOF.md);
- [`FINAL_AUDIT.md`](studies/mean_field_peeling/nonlinear_activation_operator_ide/FINAL_AUDIT.md);
- [`POST_SELECTION_INDEPENDENT_AUDIT.md`](studies/mean_field_peeling/nonlinear_activation_operator_ide/POST_SELECTION_INDEPENDENT_AUDIT.md).

---

## 1. The proved model

Let $x$ be one unit-normalized input and $y\in\mathbb R$ its label. Both
hidden layers have width $n$, and

$$
\phi(s)=\arctan s,
\qquad
\phi'(s)=\frac{1}{1+s^2}.
$$

Writing $W^{(1)},W^{(2)},W^{(3)}$ for the three trainable weight blocks,
the network can be represented along this single input as

$$
\begin{aligned}
z^{(1)}_j&=W^{(1)}_j x,\\
z^{(2)}_i&=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^n
W^{(2)}_{ij}\phi(z^{(1)}_j),\\
f_n(x)&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
W^{(3)}_i\phi(z^{(2)}_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

At initialization, the coordinates of $z^{(1)}$ and $W^{(3)}$, and the
unscaled entries of $W^{(2)}$, are mutually independent standard
Gaussians. Equivalently, if

$$
G=\frac{W^{(2)}}{\sqrt n},
$$

then $G_{ij}\sim N(0,1/n)$.

Because there is only one input, the first layer affects the loss only
through $z^{(1)}=W^{(1)}x$, and its gradient update is parallel to $x$.
Using $z^{(1)}$ as the effective trainable first-layer coordinate is
therefore exact, not a frozen-layer approximation.

The parameter metric is part of the theorem. The readout and first-layer
preactivation blocks use the normalized vector metric

$$
\langle a,b\rangle_n=\frac1n a^{\mathsf T}b,
$$

while $G$ uses the ordinary Frobenius metric. These are precisely the
layerwise mean-field feature-learning scalings after their powers of $n$
have been absorbed into the metric. Every block is trained by gradient flow
on

$$
\mathcal L_n=(y-f_n)^2.
$$

Changing this metric, freezing a layer, or replacing a reused transpose by
an independent Gaussian matrix would define a different model.

---

## 2. The continuous state

Let $(\Omega_1,\mu_1)$ label the first hidden population and
$(\Omega_2,\mu_2)$ the second. The measures $\mu_1,\mu_2$ are fixed
probability measures on label spaces; they are neither Gaussian densities
nor time-dependent distributions. Gaussianity appears through the initial
coordinate fields and the fixed wiring source described below.

The evolving state is

$$
w_{t,\alpha},\qquad r_{t,\beta},\qquad
q_{t,\alpha\beta},\qquad e_t,
$$

with the following types:

- $w_t\in L^2(\Omega_2,\mu_2)$ is the readout field;
- $r_t\in L^2(\Omega_1,\mu_1)$ is a transformed first-layer field;
- $q_t$ is one trace-class map from the first population to the second,
  represented by the ordinary square-integrable kernel
  $q_{t,\alpha\beta}$;
- $e_t\in\mathbb R$ is the residual.

Thus $q$ is the only evolving field with two population labels. The rank
needed to approximate $q_t$ numerically may increase, but the mathematical
state always contains one object of the same type, just as a PDE continues
to contain one function even if a finer numerical grid is later required.

There is also one immutable source

$$
\gamma_{\alpha\beta}.
$$

It is not an ordinary square-integrable random surface. It denotes the
canonical limiting action of the initial Gaussian matrix and its actual
transpose on every finite adaptive computation generated by the network.
In particular, it defines a bounded map and its genuine adjoint, with

$$
\left|
\int_{\Omega_2}\int_{\Omega_1}
a_\alpha\gamma_{\alpha\beta}b_\beta
\,d\mu_1(\beta)d\mu_2(\alpha)
\right|
\leq
2\|a\|_{L^2(\mu_2)}\|b\|_{L^2(\mu_1)}.
$$

This inequality records boundedness, but it is not the full definition of
the source. The full marked source also remembers the joint laws of its
actions with the Gaussian initial coordinate fields. That stronger
two-sided marked law is what prevents an incorrect replacement of
$\gamma^*$ by a fresh independent Gaussian action.

The source is fixed—or, equivalently, canonically realized—once before
training and then held fixed. It depends on neither $y$, the learning
rate, nor the future trajectory.

---

## 3. The autonomous IDE

Suppress the common time argument on the right-hand sides. Define the
first-layer preactivation implicitly by

$$
r_\beta=z^{(1)}_\beta+\frac{(z^{(1)}_\beta)^3}{3}.
$$

This relation has a unique real solution for every $r_\beta$. It is the
natural coordinate associated with arctangent because

$$
\frac{d}{dz}\left(z+\frac{z^3}{3}\right)
=\frac1{\phi'(z)}.
$$

The second-layer preactivation is

$$
z^{(2)}_\alpha
=
\int_{\Omega_1}
\bigl(\gamma_{\alpha\beta}+q_{\alpha\beta}\bigr)
\phi(z^{(1)}_\beta)d\mu_1(\beta).
$$

Integrals containing $q$ are ordinary kernel integrals. Integrals
containing $\gamma$ mean application of the fixed generalized Gaussian
action just defined.

The current predictor is

$$
f=
\int_{\Omega_2}
w_\alpha\phi(z^{(2)}_\alpha)d\mu_2(\alpha).
$$

The current tangent kernel is

$$
\begin{aligned}
K={}&
\int_{\Omega_2}\phi(z^{(2)}_\alpha)^2d\mu_2(\alpha)\\
&+
\left(
\int_{\Omega_2}
\bigl[w_\alpha\phi'(z^{(2)}_\alpha)\bigr]^2d\mu_2(\alpha)
\right)
\left(
\int_{\Omega_1}
\phi(z^{(1)}_\beta)^2d\mu_1(\beta)
\right)\\
&+
\int_{\Omega_1}
\left[
\phi'(z^{(1)}_\beta)
\int_{\Omega_2}
\bigl(\gamma_{\alpha\beta}+q_{\alpha\beta}\bigr)
w_\alpha\phi'(z^{(2)}_\alpha)d\mu_2(\alpha)
\right]^2d\mu_1(\beta).
\end{aligned}
$$

The three lines are respectively the squared gradient contributions of the
readout, the middle weight matrix, and the first layer. Hence $K\geq0$.

The limiting physical training law is

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\dot w_\alpha
&=2\eta e\,\phi(z^{(2)}_\alpha),\\[1mm]
\dot r_\beta
&=2\eta e
\int_{\Omega_2}
\bigl(\gamma_{\alpha\beta}+q_{\alpha\beta}\bigr)
w_\alpha\phi'(z^{(2)}_\alpha)d\mu_2(\alpha),\\[1mm]
\dot q_{\alpha\beta}
&=2\eta e\,
w_\alpha\phi'(z^{(2)}_\alpha)
\phi(z^{(1)}_\beta),\\[1mm]
\dot e&=-2\eta eK.
\end{aligned}}
$$

Equivalently, the learned connectivity is

$$
q_{t,\alpha\beta}
=
\int_0^t
2\eta e_s
w_{s,\alpha}\phi'(z^{(2)}_{s,\alpha})
\phi(z^{(1)}_{s,\beta})\,ds.
$$

This is the integral part of the IDE. It does not expose the past to the
future evolution: the vector field queries only the current $q_t$, never
the times at which its components were created. Retaining $q_t$ is the
Markovian compression of the complete learned matrix update. Eliminating
it would recreate a history integral.

The initial conditions are

$$
\begin{gathered}
w_{0,\alpha}\sim N(0,1),
\qquad
z^{(1)}_{0,\beta}\sim N(0,1),\\
r_{0,\beta}
=z^{(1)}_{0,\beta}+\frac{(z^{(1)}_{0,\beta})^3}{3},
\qquad
q_{0,\alpha\beta}=0,
\qquad
e_0=y.
\end{gathered}
$$

The two Gaussian coordinate fields and the fixed source are mutually
independent in the marked-source sense. The limiting initial predictor is
zero, so $e_0=y-f_0=y$.

There are no boundary conditions in $\alpha$ or $\beta$. These symbols
label populations; the equation contains no derivative with respect to
either label. The only boundary data are the initial conditions at $t=0$.

Every quantity on the right-hand side is reconstructed from the current
state and the immutable source. Every evolving object has exactly one
training-time coordinate.

---

## 4. The theorem

The IDE has a unique global physical-time solution in the canonical
Gaussian-envelope class, for every learning rate $\eta>0$ and label
$y\in\mathbb R$. Its feature-time version is also globally well posed.

Let $f_n(t)$ and $K_n(t)$ be the predictor and raw tangent kernel of the
finite network trained under the model above. Let $f(t)$, $K(t)$, and
$e(t)$ be the direct current-state readouts of the IDE. Then for every
fixed $T<\infty$,

$$
\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
\left(
|f_n(t)-f(t)|
+|K_n(t)-K(t)|
+|(y-f_n(t))^2-e(t)^2|
\right)
\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathbb P}0.
$$

Consequently the finite residual also converges uniformly in probability,
and the limiting readouts satisfy

$$
e=y-f,
\qquad
\mathcal L=e^2,
\qquad
\dot{\mathcal L}=-4\eta K\mathcal L.
$$

The result remains true after multiplying $\arctan$ by any fixed positive
constant, including the normalization that gives unit Gaussian output
variance, provided every occurrence and the natural coordinate are rescaled
consistently.

The theorem is compact-time in the width limit. Global well-posedness of
the limiting trajectory does not by itself prove that $e(t)\to0$ as
$t\to\infty$; long-time interpolation requires an additional lower bound
on the accumulated tangent kernel.

---

## 5. Why this is an $O(1)$-field law

The phrase $O(1)$ does not mean that the limit is a scalar ODE or that it
can be stored with finitely many floating-point numbers. It means that the
number and mathematical types of state variables are independent of width
and elapsed training time:

$$
\text{two one-population fields}
+\text{one two-population operator}
+\text{one scalar}.
$$

The fixed Gaussian source is infinite-dimensional, and $q_t$ is an
infinite-dimensional current operator. Neither is a disguised width-$n$
matrix: they live on population spaces fixed before the limit, and the
finite networks converge to their marked action law rather than to an
operator-norm embedding of matrices.

The distinction from a two-time theory is structural. A response kernel
$R(t,s)$ creates a new slice of state for every past time $s\leq t$.
Here $q_t$ has only the current time $t$. The future can be restarted from

$$
(w_t,r_t,q_t,e_t)
$$

and the same immutable source $\gamma$, without retaining the path used to
reach that state.

The theorem therefore gives a causal macroscopic law, not merely a compact
encoding of one already known loss curve.

---

## 6. Why the proof closes

Five ideas are jointly decisive.

### 6.1 The natural coordinate

For a general first-layer preactivation, backpropagation introduces the
multiplier $\phi'(z^{(1)})$. Arctangent admits the global change of
coordinate

$$
r=z^{(1)}+\frac{(z^{(1)})^3}{3},
$$

which removes that multiplier exactly from the evolution of $r$. This is
an invertible reparameterization of the original gradient flow, not a change
of optimizer.

### 6.2 Bounded forward features

Because $\arctan$ and its derivative are bounded, the readout changes by a
bounded pointwise amount over a compact feature-time interval. Its Gaussian
tail is translated rather than amplified into the rare-coordinate boundary
layer that obstructed the quadratic activation.

### 6.3 A static two-sided Gaussian action

The same initial matrix is reused adaptively in forward and transpose
directions. A fresh-Gaussian approximation would erase a real correlation.
The finite two-sided tensor-program master theorem identifies every fixed
Euler discretization, including singular query-Gram cases. A countable
projective construction and the Gaussian spectral-norm limit then produce
one deterministic marked source with a genuine adjoint.

### 6.4 A current trace-class update

Every matrix update is rank one. Their time integral is the single current
trace-class operator $q_t$. This closes the algebra without introducing a
time-indexed decomposition.

### 6.5 Tail transfer before mesh removal

The raw kernel contains the square of an adaptive transpose action. A bare
$L^2$ bound is insufficient, and an earlier proof attempt incorrectly
multiplied a shrinking mesh error by a high-moment constant that could grow
as the mesh shrank. The repaired proof first obtains square-tail tightness
for the exact continuous cutoff trajectory from one fixed auxiliary mesh.
It then removes a separate comparison mesh by truncation, and finally
removes the Gaussian readout cutoff. No mesh-uniform high moment or
leave-one-out lemma is assumed.

Together with dimension-free Euler stability, Gaussian cutoff comparison,
Osgood uniqueness, and the scalar physical-time clock, these steps identify
the finite-width dynamics with the autonomous IDE.

---

## 7. What has not been proved

The theorem does not yet cover:

- two or more training samples;
- three or more nonlinear hidden layers;
- a general nonlinear activation class;
- a continuum distribution of inputs;
- an infinite-time interpolation theorem;
- a Gram-only autonomous closure;
- a finite-dimensional scalar state;
- arbitrary deterministic spike initializations;
- operator-norm convergence of finite matrices;
- or a theory of biological or general intelligence.

It is also not a DMFT result rewritten in different notation. No two-time
response object occurs in either the statement or proof.

---

## 8. Extension program

The target is a master theorem for arbitrary fixed depth, arbitrary fixed
sample configuration, and a broad regular activation class, while retaining
the same strict contract:

> A width-independent finite collection of current fields/operators, one
> training-time coordinate, no stored history, direct current-state
> observables, restartability, and compact-time convergence of the finite
> mean-field feature-learning network.

The most efficient route is not to generalize one axis completely in
isolation. It is to solve a sequence of crux models that isolate the new
obstruction introduced by each axis and then test their compatibility.

### 8.1 First finish the depth crux and extract its reusable mechanism

At hidden depth three, the exact candidate contains

- one immutable Gaussian action and one current trace-class perturbation for
  each inter-hidden-layer matrix;
- current forward fields propagated from bottom to top;
- current damped cotangent fields propagated from top to bottom;
- the readout and residual.

The number of species is $O(L)$ for fixed hidden depth $L$, independent of
width and elapsed training time. All fields have one current training-time
coordinate.

For $L=3$, the finite feature-gradient equations and the four-term tangent
kernel identity have now been independently derived and checked at finite
width. The exact autonomous operator candidate and every fixed-mesh
two-matrix source program are also established. The unconditional
continuous-time convergence theorem remains open. Its decisive issue is
control of an adaptive middle transpose acting on a current backpropagated
field. Arctangent damping shows that the dangerous coefficients are the
current cotangents, not the unbounded readout in isolation.  The completed
isolated routes have ruled out bare (L^2/L^1) topology, finite cotangent and
Jacobian lifts, ordinary layerwise cutoff, first-response Gaussian
integration by parts, absolute Fock/response norms, fixed-(p) restart, and
uniformly equivalent moving-coordinate repairs as sufficient black-box
arguments.  None of those route failures is a reachable iid-Gaussian

paired-block dynamic low-influence estimate for the middle static adjoint
(and the induced lower raw square); it need not imply row delocalization.

### 8.2 The data-and-representation crux

The next genuinely different mechanism is shared training over more than
one input. For $B$ samples, each input-dependent forward or backward field
acquires $B$ current channels. The readout and learned operators remain
shared. The input Gram matrix specifies the initial joint Gaussian law and
the covariant first-layer update. Predictions and residuals become vectors,
with

$$
\dot e_a=-\frac{2\eta}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B K_{ab}e_b.
$$

The smallest nondegenerate crux is

$$
L=2,\qquad B=2,\qquad x_1^{\mathsf T}x_2=\tfrac12,
\qquad \phi=\arctan,
$$

with arbitrary labels and with equal-label and opposite-label choices used
as complementary audits. Correlation zero can conceal coupling, while
correlation one collapses the two inputs into a degenerate case.

This crux should include the forward activation Gram at each hidden layer:

$$
C^{(\ell)}_{ab}(t)
=
\int_{\Omega_\ell}
\phi\!\left(z^{(\ell)}_{a,\alpha}(t)\right)
\phi\!\left(z^{(\ell)}_{b,\alpha}(t)\right)
\,d\mu_\ell(\alpha).
$$

For one input this is only a scalar self-norm, which can be added to the
proved theorem as an easy readout but contains little representation
geometry. With two inputs, the off-diagonal entry is the first observable of
learned similarity or separation. These bounded Grams should remain direct
current-state readouts, not additional dynamical variables. Their velocities
should also be reconstructed from the current IDE, exposing the exact
representation--prediction cross-mobility.

The required deliverable is therefore not merely a two-sample predictor
law. It is an autonomous convergence theorem for the predictor vector, raw
tangent-kernel matrix, residual, loss, and both hidden activation Grams.

### 8.3 The depth--data compatibility test

After the one-input depth theorem and the two-input depth-two theorem are
separately understood, they must be combined in

$$
L=3,\qquad B=2,\qquad \phi=\arctan.
$$

This is an essential integration test. Separate success along two axes does
not prove that sample summation preserves damped-cotangent tails through
recursive transpose reuse. The model must verify simultaneously that

- the multi-input natural-coordinate estimates survive another trained
  matrix;
- adaptive cotangent bounds survive correlated sample channels;
- raw tangent-kernel and Gram convergence hold together;
- and no response history or second training time is introduced.

Only after this compatibility test passes should the arctangent master
theorem be proved for arbitrary fixed $L$ and $B$, arbitrary fixed labels,
and arbitrary input Gram matrices, including correlated and singular cases.
The limiting state then has $O(L)$ field/operator species and $B$ current
data channels; its complexity is independent of width and training time.

### 8.4 Broaden the activation only after the architecture is stable

Arctangent is not expected to be unique. It is the cleanest proved nonlinear
member because it combines bounded smooth output, a derivative that never
vanishes, a global natural coordinate, and a polynomially transformed
Gaussian initialization. For a strictly monotone activation, the analogous
coordinate is

$$
\Theta(u)=\int_0^u\frac{ds}{\phi'(s)}.
$$

This algebraic transformation alone is not a convergence theorem. The
transformed initialization must remain in the Gaussian source class, and
all adaptively generated forward and cotangent fields must have sufficient
compact-time tail control.

Boundedness should not be imposed as a final principle. Identity is
unbounded and already has exact autonomous closures. The first nonlinear
unbounded crux should therefore be

$$
\phi(x)=x+\lambda\tanh x,\qquad \lambda>0.
$$

It has linear growth, bounded smooth derivatives, and a derivative bounded
away from zero. It directly tests whether bounded forward activation was
essential or merely convenient. The activation should pass through the same
minimal ladder:

1. $L=2$, one input;
2. $L=3$, one input;
3. $L=2$, two correlated inputs;
4. $L=3$, two correlated inputs.

The hypotheses of the eventual activation class should be inferred from
these proofs rather than guessed in advance. Plausible ingredients are at
most linear growth, bounded sufficiently regular derivatives, a tame global
natural coordinate, controlled transformed initialization, and stable
damping of cotangent fields. Activations with kinks, strong derivative
degeneracy, or nonmonotonicity may require separate mechanisms.

The next master theorem would then cover every fixed $L$, fixed $B$, compact
time horizon, and activation in the verified class, while retaining the same
single-time autonomous state contract.

### 8.5 Enlarge the observable theory

Forward activation Grams enter at the two-input crux rather than being
postponed until the end. After they are established, observables should be
added in increasing order of analytic difficulty:

1. preactivation Grams and moments;
2. backward-sensitivity Grams;
3. layerwise tangent-kernel contributions;
4. representation--prediction cross-mobilities;
5. singular-value or spectral statistics of learned operators;
6. the induced movement cost and geometry of Gram trajectories.

Each object should first be treated as a readout of the existing current
state. It becomes a new state variable only if its future is genuinely not
reconstructible from that state. Bounded current readouts should follow from
field convergence; raw quadratic or spectral observables require their own
uniform-integrability or continuity audit.

### 8.6 Pass from finite data to a data distribution

After estimates for fixed $B$ have been made uniform in the number of data
atoms, replace the batch by a distribution $\rho(dx,dy)$ on a
fixed-dimensional input space. Population-gradient flow replaces sample sums
by integrals over $x$. Current fields acquire an input coordinate, and the
tangent kernel becomes $K_t(x,x')$.

The two arguments $x,x'$ are data coordinates, not two training times. Every
evolving object still has only the current time $t$. The intended proof is
finite atomic approximation followed by an atom-count-uniform stability and
tail limit. Infinite or continuous depth should be considered only after
this data-distribution theorem; arbitrary fixed depth is the nearer target.

### 8.7 Dependency-ordered roadmap

The frozen sequence after completion of the present $L=3$ crux is:

1. extract the $L=3$ source, cotangent, mesh, and tail lemmas;
2. verify the induction at $L=4$ and prove arctangent for one input and
   arbitrary fixed $L$;
3. prove $L=2$, two correlated inputs, including both hidden activation
   Grams;
4. pass the $L=3$, two-input depth--data compatibility test;
5. prove the arctangent master theorem for arbitrary fixed $L$ and $B$;
6. solve the linearly growing nonlinear activation crux and infer the actual
   admissible activation class;
7. prove the fixed-$L$, fixed-$B$ master theorem for that class;
8. extend the readout theory to backward, layerwise-kernel, spectral, and
   Gram-mobility observables;
9. pass to input distributions through atom-count-uniform estimates;
10. investigate long-time interpolation, implicit bias, and the quotient
    geometry of learned representations.

At every stage, exact finite algebra, genuine reused transposes,
well-posedness, compact-time finite-width convergence, the raw tangent
kernel, restartability, and the absence of hidden time memory remain
acceptance gates. A formal IDE or successful finite computation does not by
itself promote an extension to theorem status.

## 9. An exact variational structure already inside the theorem

The autonomous IDE is not merely compatible with decreasing loss. It is
the original gradient flow written on its limiting state space.

Let

$$
U=(w,r,q)
$$

denote the independent evolving state; $e=y-f(U)$ is then derived. For a
state perturbation $\delta U=(\delta w,\delta r,\delta q)$, define the
network-inherited squared length

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\delta U\|_{g,U}^2
={}&
\int_{\Omega_2}(\delta w_\alpha)^2d\mu_2(\alpha)\\
&+
\int_{\Omega_1}
\bigl[\phi'(z^{(1)}_\beta)\delta r_\beta\bigr]^2
d\mu_1(\beta)
+\|\delta q\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The state dependence in the second term is exactly the metric change caused
by replacing $z^{(1)}$ with $r=z^{(1)}+(z^{(1)})^3/3$. With respect to
this metric,

$$
\dot U=-\eta\,\operatorname{grad}_{g}(y-f(U))^2.
$$

Moreover,

$$
K=\|\operatorname{grad}_{g}f\|_{g}^{2}.
$$

Thus the tangent kernel is the squared speed with which the predictor can
move in the inherited geometry.

At each current state, the physical velocity obeys the exact
minimum-dissipation principle

$$
\dot U
=
\underset{V}{\arg\min}
\left\{
D\mathcal L(U)[V]
+\frac1{2\eta}\|V\|_{g,U}^2
\right\}.
$$

The whole trajectory also minimizes the energy-dissipation functional. For
every sufficiently regular competing path $V_t$ with $V_0=U_0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathcal L(V_T)
+\frac1{2\eta}\int_0^T\|\dot V_t\|_{g,V_t}^2dt
+\frac\eta2\int_0^T
\|\operatorname{grad}_{g}\mathcal L(V_t)\|_{g,V_t}^2dt
-\mathcal L(V_0)\\
&\qquad=
\frac1{2\eta}\int_0^T
\|\dot V_t+\eta\operatorname{grad}_{g}\mathcal L(V_t)\|_{g,V_t}^2dt
\geq0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Gradient flow is precisely the path that makes the right-hand side zero.
This is a rigorous minimum-action statement, but it is a minimum-dissipation
action for the complete path. It does not say that the endpoint is the
globally nearest interpolating representation or the minimizer of an
unknown static Gram energy.

For the one-sample theorem there is an additional simplification: physical
training follows the same geometric feature-ascent orbit and the residual
only changes the speed along that orbit. A genuine label geometry appears
only once several inputs and labels are present.
